keyVerseText: And all the people of the land went into the house of Baal, and brake it down; his altars and his images brake they in pieces thoroughly, and slew Mattan the priest of Baal before the altars. And the priest appointed officers over the house of the LORD. officers: Heb. offices
rootMeaning: The Hebrew word מַתָּן (Mattân) originates from the root מַתָּן (H4976), which conveys the idea of a gift, giving, or reward. This root emphasizes the concept of a present or offering, highlighting the act of bestowing something valuable. Beyond the common English gloss 'gift,' the root sense carries a nuance of intentionality and generosity, underscoring the relational aspect of giving as a meaningful exchange rather than a mere object.
usageInScripture: The word מַתָּן appears three times in Scripture, primarily as a proper name. It is most notably used to refer to a priest of Baal in Jerusalem during the time of Athaliah, and also as the name of an Israelite father of Shephatiah in Jeremiah's time. The top translations consistently render it as 'Mattan' or 'of Mattan,' indicating its function as a personal name rather than a common noun in these contexts. This usage reveals the word's dual role as both a meaningful noun and a proper name within biblical narratives.
theologicalSignificance: Understanding מַתָּן as 'gift' enriches our grasp of Scripture by reminding believers that God’s blessings and spiritual endowments are gracious gifts rather than earned merits. The fact that this term also identifies a priest of Baal serves as a sober reminder of the contrast between true worship and idolatry. Theologically, it invites reflection on the nature of divine offerings — God’s grace is the ultimate gift, freely given and unmerited. This insight encourages faith rooted in gratitude and dependence on God’s generous provision rather than human effort or false religious systems.
keyVerseReflection: In 2 Kings 11:18, the text recounts how the people destroyed the house of Baal and killed Mattan, the priest of Baal, before the altars. The name 'Mattan' here is significant as it contrasts the idea of a 'gift' with the idolatrous worship he represented. The verse highlights the decisive rejection of false gifts and worship, underscoring the people's return to true worship under the LORD. Thus, the word 'Mattan' deepens the narrative by embodying the conflict between genuine divine blessing and counterfeit religious practices.
